content: The global rate of caesarean sections is increasing, and the factors driving this trend are multifaceted. Non-clinical interventions, which are implemented outside the direct clinical interaction between healthcare providers and patients, aim to address the underlying determinants of caesarean births. These interventions may target women, their families, healthcare professionals, or healthcare organizations, and they hold potential for reducing unnecessary caesarean sections. This review, originally published in 2011, has been updated to inform a new World Health Organization (WHO) guideline. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness and safety of non-clinical interventions designed to reduce unnecessary caesarean sections. A comprehensive search was conducted in March 2018 across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and CINAHL, as well as trial registries and relevant organizational websites. Eligible studies included randomized trials, non-randomized trials, controlled before-and-after studies, interrupted time series studies, and repeated measures studies. The primary outcomes assessed were caesarean section rates, spontaneous vaginal births, and instrumental births. The review included 29 studies, comprising 19 randomized trials, one controlled before-and-after study, and nine interrupted time series studies. Most studies were conducted in high-income countries, with no studies from low-income settings. The participants included a diverse population of pregnant women, such as nulliparous women, multiparous women, women with a fear of childbirth, women with high anxiety levels, and women with a history of previous caesarean sections. Interventions Targeted at Women or Families 1. Childbirth Training Workshops for Mothers Alone: These workshops may reduce caesarean section rates (risk ratio [RR] 0.55, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.33 to 0.89) and increase spontaneous vaginal births (RR 2.25, 95% CI 1.16 to 4.36). However, the evidence is of low certainty. 2. Childbirth Training Workshops for Couples: These workshops may also reduce caesarean section rates (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.94) and increase spontaneous vaginal births (RR 2.13, 95% CI 1.09 to 4.16). The evidence for these outcomes is of low certainty, based on a single study with 60 participants. 3. Nurse-Led Applied Relaxation Training: This intervention may significantly reduce caesarean section rates (RR 0.22, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.43; 104 participants), but the evidence is of low certainty. 4. Psychosocial Couple-Based Prevention Programs: These programs may reduce caesarean section rates (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.90; 147 participants), with low-certainty evidence. 5. Psychoeducation: This intervention may increase spontaneous vaginal births (RR 1.33, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.61; 371 participants), but the evidence is of low certainty. In all these studies, the control groups received routine maternity care. There was insufficient data to assess the impact of these interventions on maternal and neonatal mortality or morbidity. Interventions Targeted at Healthcare Professionals 1. Implementation of Clinical Practice Guidelines with Mandatory Second Opinions: This approach slightly reduces overall caesarean section rates (mean difference in rate change: -1.9%, 95% CI -3.8 to -0.1; 149,223 participants). The evidence is of high certainty. 2. Implementation of Clinical Practice Guidelines with Audit and Feedback: This intervention also slightly reduces caesarean section rates (risk difference [RD] -1.8%, 95% CI -3.8 to -0.2; 105,351 participants). The evidence is of high certainty. 3. Physician Education by Local Opinion Leaders: Education provided by obstetrician-gynecologists acting as local opinion leaders reduced the rate of elective caesarean sections from 66.8% to 53.7% (opinion leader education: 53.7%, 95% CI 46.5 to 61.0%; control: 66.8%, 95% CI 61.7 to 72.0%; 2496 participants). The evidence is of high certainty. In these studies, healthcare professionals in the control groups received routine care. There was little or no difference in maternal and neonatal mortality or morbidity between the intervention and control groups. Interventions Targeted at Healthcare Organizations or Facilities 1. Collaborative Midwifery-Labourist Care: This model, where obstetricians provide 24-hour in-house labor and delivery coverage without competing clinical duties, may reduce primary caesarean section rates. In one interrupted time series study, the caesarean section rate decreased by 7% in the year following the intervention and by 1.7% per year thereafter (1722 participants). The vaginal birth rate after caesarean section increased from 13.3% to 22.4% (684 participants). However, the evidence is of low certainty, and maternal and neonatal mortality were not reported. Interventions with Little or No Effect Moderate-certainty evidence suggests that the following interventions have little or no effect on caesarean section rates: Antenatal education programs for physiologic childbirth. Antenatal education on natural childbirth preparation, including breathing and relaxation techniques. Computer-based decision aids. Individualized prenatal education and support programs compared to written information in pamphlets. Low-certainty evidence suggests little or no effect on caesarean section rates for: Psychoeducation. Pelvic floor muscle training exercises with telephone follow-up compared to training without follow-up. Intensive group therapy, including cognitive behavioral therapy and childbirth psychotherapy. Education of public health nurses on childbirth classes. Role-playing compared to standard education using lectures. Interactive decision aids compared to educational brochures. Labourist models of obstetric care compared to traditional models. The effects of other identified interventions on caesarean section rates remain highly uncertain due to very low-certainty evidence. Authors' Conclusions This review evaluated a broad range of non-clinical interventions aimed at reducing unnecessary caesarean sections, primarily in high-income settings. Only a few interventions, particularly those targeting healthcare professionals (e.g., implementation of guidelines with mandatory second opinions, audit and feedback, and physician education by local opinion leaders), demonstrated moderateor high-certainty evidence of effectiveness in safely reducing caesarean section rates. However, there are significant uncertainties in the existing evidence, particularly regarding interventions targeting women, families, and healthcare organizations. Additionally, there is a lack of studies conducted in low-income settings, limiting the generalizability of the findings.
